newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein tells Catholics "take to the streets".
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein tells Catholics "take to the streets".

text.p: A leader of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, urged Northern Ireland Catholics on Sunday to "take to the streets" to protest against the holding of an Orange Order parade in Portadown.
Martin McGuinness, chief negotiator for the party, told a rally in Northern Ireland's second city that Catholics should "stand up for their rights".

McGuinness, whose party seeks the end of British rule of Northern Ireland, said the people of Londonderry, who are mainly Catholic Irish nationalists, were like "the people of Chile, Nicaragua, El Salvador and South Africa.
"The place to be demanding justice is on the streets confronting your opponents," he said to wild applause.

Shortly before he spoke police reported two shooting incidents in Belfast and Coalisland, north of Portadown, which were believed to be the work of the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and an allied movement fighting British rule of the province.
In one, a policewoman was injured in the face but not seriously wounded by a man armed with a shotgun. In the second a masked man fired at a police patrol in Belfast but missed.

Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, was addressing a similar rally in Belfast at about the same time. The rallies were followed by a spate of car hijackings in Catholic areas and disturbances in nationalist parts of Belfast, Lurgan and elsewhere.

McGuinness, whose party is demanding unconditional entry into Northern Ireland peace talks from which it is barred because of IRA violence, told nationalists to make their anger over the Portadown parade heard.
"The turnout in the Six Counties (Northern Ireland) over the next couple of weeks will show the Nationalist Community is determined to get justice and peace for the people of Ireland," he said.
The next two weeks see the climax of the Protestant "marching season" which Catholics say is intimidation and which Protestants say is a birthright.
Leaders of the Order say they want only to "march along the Queen's highway" to celebrate their British way of life and allegiance to their faith and the province's British status.
But McGuinness said the holding of the parade showed that the British government had no respect for Catholic rights and praised demonstrators of Portadown's Garvaghy Road for protesting against it.
"We the people of (London)Derry salute them from the bottom of our hearts," he said.

Londonderry is regarded as the birthplace of militant Irish nationalism after civil rights marches in the 1970s exploded into violence at the onset of the 28-year political and sectarian strife known as Northern Ireland's "Troubles."
Some 3,200 have been killed in a war involving the security forces, the IRA and its Protestant Loyalist foes who want the province to remain British.

McGuinness and Adams were elected to the British parliament in May 1 polls, which returned the Labour government of Tony Blair, but refused to take their seats because it would entail an oath of allegiance to Britain.
McGuinness said Blair's government had "failed its first test miserably" by allowing the Portadown march to take place.

Blair offered Sinn Fein a seat at Northern Ireland peace talks within six weeks if it called a new, credible truce to its guerrilla war against Britain. But the violence appears to have buried hopes of any imminent ceasefire.
